title: Promise, Prayer, and Pentecost
lesson: Luke opens Acts with Jesus’ forty days of appearances and a clear commission: wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit, then be witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. After the ascension, about 120 believers devote themselves to prayer, and Matthias is chosen to replace Judas among the apostles.

At Pentecost the Spirit fills the disciples with wind-and-fire power. Peter proclaims the crucified and risen Christ; about three thousand repent, are baptized, and devote themselves to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer. The church’s life is Word, community, worship, and prayer—and the Lord adds to their number daily.

featuredVerse.text: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

questions.prompt: According to Acts 1:8, where would the apostles be witnesses?
choices: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and the ends of the earth
questions.explanation: Acts 1:8 maps the mission: Jerusalem → Judea/Samaria → the ends of the earth.

questions.prompt: What filled the house at Pentecost?
choices: A sound like a violent wind
questions.explanation: A sound like the blowing of a violent wind came from heaven and filled the house (Acts 2:2).

questions.prompt: About how many were added to the church on Pentecost?
questions.explanation: About three thousand were added that day (Acts 2:41).

questions.prompt: Who was chosen to replace Judas among the apostles?
questions.explanation: Lots were cast and Matthias was added to the eleven apostles (Acts 1:26).

questions.prompt: What did the early believers devote themselves to after Pentecost?
choices: The apostles’ teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer
questions.explanation: Acts 2:42 names teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer.

title: Healing, Boldness, and Shared Life
lesson: At the Beautiful Gate, Peter heals a man lame from birth in Jesus’ name. The crowd gathers, and Peter calls Israel to repent and turn to God so that times of refreshing may come from the Lord. The miracle points beyond the apostles to the risen Jesus, the Holy and Righteous One.

Arrested for preaching the resurrection, Peter tells the Sanhedrin that salvation is found in no other name under heaven. The rulers command silence, but Peter and John answer that they must speak what they have seen and heard. The church prays for boldness; the place is shaken, they speak God’s word boldly, and share so that none among them are needy.

featuredVerse.text: Salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to mankind by which we must be saved.

questions.prompt: Where was the lame man healed?
choices: At the temple gate called Beautiful
questions.explanation: Peter and John met him at the temple gate called Beautiful (Acts 3:2).

questions.prompt: In whose name did Peter heal the lame man?
questions.explanation: Peter said, “In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk” (Acts 3:6).

questions.prompt: According to Peter, in what name is salvation found?
questions.explanation: Acts 4:12: there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved.

questions.prompt: What did the believers pray for after Peter and John were released?
questions.explanation: They asked God to enable them to speak his word with great boldness (Acts 4:29).

questions.prompt: How did the early church care for needs among them?
choices: They shared so that there were no needy persons among them
questions.explanation: Believers shared possessions; there were no needy persons among them (Acts 4:34–35).

title: Integrity, Arrest, and Servant Leaders
lesson: Ananias and Sapphira lie about their gift and fall under God’s judgment—a sobering reminder that the Spirit will not be mocked. Signs and wonders continue through the apostles; crowds bring the sick, and even Peter’s shadow is sought for healing. Arrested again, the apostles are freed by an angel and told to keep teaching in the temple courts.

Before the Sanhedrin, Peter insists, “We must obey God rather than human beings.” Gamaliel urges caution, and the apostles rejoice that they were counted worthy to suffer for the Name. As the church grows, seven Spirit-filled servants—including Stephen and Philip—are chosen so the apostles can devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word.

featuredVerse.text: Peter and the other apostles replied: “We must obey God rather than human beings!”

questions.prompt: What was Ananias and Sapphira’s sin?
choices: Lying about how much of the sale they brought
questions.explanation: They kept back part of the money and lied as if they had given all (Acts 5:1–4).

questions.prompt: What did Peter tell the Sanhedrin about obedience?
choices: We must obey God rather than human beings
questions.explanation: Acts 5:29 is the apostles’ clear reply.

questions.prompt: How were the apostles freed after their arrest in Acts 5?
choices: An angel of the Lord opened the jail doors
questions.explanation: An angel opened the doors and told them to keep teaching (Acts 5:19–20).

questions.prompt: Why were seven men chosen in Acts 6?
choices: To serve neglected widows so the apostles could focus on prayer and the word
questions.explanation: The Seven were appointed for daily food distribution while the apostles devoted themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word (Acts 6:1–4).

questions.prompt: Which of these men was among the seven chosen to serve?
questions.explanation: Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, was among the seven (Acts 6:5).

title: Stephen’s Witness and a Spreading Gospel
lesson: Stephen’s Spirit-filled defense retells Israel’s story and confronts resistance to God’s messengers. Seeing heaven opened and Jesus standing at God’s right hand, he is stoned. His dying prayer echoes Jesus: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Saul watches approvingly as persecution scatters believers—and the gospel goes with them.

Philip proclaims Christ in Samaria; many believe, and there is great joy. Simon the sorcerer is rebuked for thinking the Spirit’s gift can be bought. On the desert road, Philip explains Isaiah to an Ethiopian official, baptizes him, and the man goes on his way rejoicing. Suffering does not stop the mission—it spreads it.

featuredVerse.text: Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went.

questions.prompt: What did Stephen see as he was being killed?
choices: Heaven open and Jesus standing at God’s right hand
questions.explanation: Stephen saw the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55–56).

questions.prompt: What happened after Stephen’s death?
choices: A great persecution scattered believers, who preached the word wherever they went
questions.explanation: Persecution scattered everyone except the apostles; the scattered preached the word (Acts 8:1–4).

questions.prompt: Where did Philip preach with great joy in the city?
questions.explanation: Philip went to a city in Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah (Acts 8:5–8).

questions.prompt: What book was the Ethiopian official reading?
questions.explanation: He was reading Isaiah the prophet (Acts 8:28–30).

questions.prompt: What did Philip do after explaining the good news about Jesus?
choices: Sent the man back to Jerusalem
questions.explanation: They stopped the chariot and Philip baptized him (Acts 8:36–38).

title: Saul Converted; Gentiles Welcomed
lesson: On the Damascus road a light from heaven stops Saul. The risen Jesus asks, “Why do you persecute me?” Blinded, Saul prays; Ananias lays hands on him, scales fall, and Saul is baptized. The persecutor becomes a preacher—speaking boldly in Damascus and later in Jerusalem, though many disciples still fear him.

In Caesarea, Cornelius the centurion receives a vision; in Joppa, Peter sees a sheet of unclean animals and hears, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.” Peter goes to Cornelius’s house, proclaims Jesus, and the Holy Spirit falls on Gentile hearers. They are baptized—God shows no favoritism, and the door to the nations swings open.

featuredVerse.text: Then Peter began to speak: “I now realize how true it is that God does not show favoritism but accepts from every nation the one who fears him and does what is right.”

questions.prompt: What did Jesus ask Saul on the Damascus road?
choices: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?
questions.explanation: Acts 9:4 records Jesus’ question to Saul.

questions.prompt: Who laid hands on Saul so he could see again?
questions.explanation: The Lord sent Ananias to Saul in Damascus (Acts 9:10–18).

questions.prompt: What did Peter’s vision about unclean animals teach?
choices: Do not call impure what God has made clean—preparing him for Gentile mission
questions.explanation: God’s word in the vision prepared Peter to welcome Gentiles (Acts 10:15, 28).

questions.prompt: Who was Cornelius?
choices: A Roman centurion in Caesarea who feared God
questions.explanation: Cornelius was a devout centurion in Caesarea (Acts 10:1–2).

questions.prompt: What happened while Peter was speaking at Cornelius’s house?
choices: The Spirit fell on the Gentile hearers
questions.explanation: The Holy Spirit came on all who heard the message (Acts 10:44–48).

title: Antioch, Prayer, and a Prison Door
lesson: Peter explains God’s work among the Gentiles; the Jerusalem believers glorify God that even Gentiles have been granted repentance unto life. In Antioch, scattered believers preach to Greeks; a great number believe. Barnabas fetches Saul, and for a year they teach—disciples are first called Christians there. Agabus predicts famine, and the church sends relief.

Herod kills James and imprisons Peter. The church prays earnestly; an angel wakes Peter, chains fall, and the iron gate opens by itself. Rhoda’s joy at the door almost keeps Peter outside, but the praying church sees God’s answer. Herod’s pride ends in judgment, while the word of God continues to spread and flourish.

featuredVerse.text: So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was earnestly praying to God for him.

questions.prompt: Where were believers first called Christians?
questions.explanation: The disciples were called Christians first at Antioch (Acts 11:26).

questions.prompt: How did the church respond when Peter was imprisoned?
choices: They earnestly prayed to God for him
questions.explanation: Acts 12:5 highlights the church’s earnest prayer.

questions.prompt: Who helped Peter escape from prison?
questions.explanation: An angel woke Peter and led him out (Acts 12:7–10).

questions.prompt: Which apostle did Herod put to death with the sword?
questions.explanation: Herod had James, the brother of John, put to death (Acts 12:2).

questions.prompt: What did Antioch believers do when Agabus predicted famine?
choices: Provided help for the brothers and sisters in Judea
questions.explanation: The disciples sent relief to Judea by Barnabas and Saul (Acts 11:28–30).

title: Sent Out: The First Missionary Journey
lesson: In Antioch the Holy Spirit says, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul.” After fasting and prayer, the church sends them. On Cyprus they confront Elymas; in Pisidian Antioch Paul proclaims Jesus from Israel’s story—forgiveness and freedom through Christ. Many rejoice; others stir persecution, and the missionaries shake the dust from their feet.

In Iconium and Lystra they keep preaching. At Lystra a lame man is healed; the crowd tries to worship Paul and Barnabas as gods, then turns and stones Paul. Yet he rises and continues. Returning through the cities, they strengthen disciples, appoint elders with prayer and fasting, and report to Antioch all that God had done—especially how he opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

featuredVerse.text: While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.”

questions.prompt: Who set apart Barnabas and Saul for mission?
questions.explanation: The Holy Spirit said to set them apart (Acts 13:2).

questions.prompt: What island did they visit early in the journey?
questions.explanation: They sailed to Cyprus (Acts 13:4).

questions.prompt: In Pisidian Antioch, what did Paul proclaim was available through Jesus?
questions.explanation: Through Jesus, forgiveness of sins is proclaimed (Acts 13:38–39).

questions.prompt: What happened to Paul at Lystra after the healing?
choices: Crowds tried to worship him, then later stoned him
questions.explanation: They called them gods, then opponents stoned Paul (Acts 14:11–19).

questions.prompt: What did Paul and Barnabas do on the return trip?
choices: Returned only by sea in secret
questions.explanation: They strengthened believers and appointed elders in each church (Acts 14:21–23).

title: Council, Macedonia, and a Midnight Song
lesson: Debate arises: must Gentile believers be circumcised? In Jerusalem, Peter recalls Cornelius; Paul and Barnabas report signs among the Gentiles; James cites the prophets. The council affirms salvation by grace and sends a letter of welcome with a few wise practices for fellowship. Unity in the gospel is guarded with clarity and kindness.

Paul and Silas take the Macedonian call. In Philippi, Lydia’s heart opens; a slave girl’s freedom sparks a riot; Paul and Silas are beaten and jailed. At midnight they pray and sing hymns—then an earthquake opens doors. The jailer asks, “What must I do to be saved?” They answer, “Believe in the Lord Jesus,” and his household rejoices in baptism.

featuredVerse.text: They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.”

questions.prompt: What major question did the Jerusalem Council address?
choices: Whether Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved
Whether to build a new temple
questions.explanation: Some taught circumcision was required; the council settled the matter (Acts 15:1–11).

questions.prompt: How are people saved, according to Peter at the council?
choices: Through the grace of the Lord Jesus
questions.explanation: Peter says we believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved (Acts 15:11).

questions.prompt: What vision redirected Paul toward Europe?
choices: A man of Macedonia begging him to come help
questions.explanation: The Macedonian vision called them to preach there (Acts 16:9–10).

questions.prompt: What did Paul and Silas do at midnight in prison?
choices: Prayed and sang hymns to God
questions.explanation: About midnight they were praying and singing hymns (Acts 16:25).

questions.prompt: What answer did they give the jailer about salvation?
choices: Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved
questions.explanation: Acts 16:31 is their clear gospel reply.

title: Cities, Idols, and Tentmaking
lesson: In Thessalonica and Berea, Paul reasons from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise. Bereans examine the word daily with eagerness. In Athens, Paul addresses the Areopagus: God made the world, gives life and breath, and now commands all people everywhere to repent—because he has set a day to judge the world by the risen Jesus.

In Corinth, Paul works with Aquila and Priscilla as tentmakers and stays a year and a half teaching the word. The Lord encourages him in a night vision not to be afraid. Gallio dismisses charges against him. Apollos, eloquent and fervent, is gently instructed more accurately by Priscilla and Aquila, then powerfully helps believers. The gospel advances through Scripture, friendship, and courage.

featuredVerse.text: In the past God overlooked such ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent. For he has set a day when he will judge the world with justice by the man he has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead.

questions.prompt: What were the Bereans known for?
choices: Examining the Scriptures daily to see if Paul’s message was true
questions.explanation: They received the message eagerly and examined the Scriptures daily (Acts 17:11).

questions.prompt: In Athens, what did Paul say God now commands all people to do?
questions.explanation: God commands all people everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30).

questions.prompt: What trade did Paul practice with Aquila and Priscilla?
questions.explanation: They were tentmakers by trade (Acts 18:3).

questions.prompt: How long did Paul stay teaching in Corinth?
questions.explanation: He stayed for a year and a half, teaching them the word of God (Acts 18:11).

questions.prompt: Who helped Apollos understand the way of God more accurately?
questions.explanation: Priscilla and Aquila explained the way of God more adequately (Acts 18:26).

title: Ephesus, Idols, and Shepherds of the Flock
lesson: In Ephesus, disciples who knew only John’s baptism receive the Holy Spirit when Paul lays hands on them. The word spreads mightily; many who practiced magic burn their scrolls. Demetrius the silversmith stirs a riot for Artemis, but the city clerk calms the crowd. The gospel challenges idols and livelihoods built on them.

Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, raises Eutychus at Troas, and hurries toward Jerusalem. At Miletus he meets the Ephesian elders: he has not hesitated to preach the whole counsel of God; they must keep watch over themselves and the flock; God bought the church with his own blood. With tears and prayer he commits them to God and the word of his grace.

featuredVerse.text: Keep watch over yourselves and all the flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which he bought with his own blood.

questions.prompt: What did many former magicians in Ephesus do?
choices: Brought their scrolls together and burned them
questions.explanation: They burned their scrolls publicly (Acts 19:19).

questions.prompt: Why did Demetrius stir up trouble in Ephesus?
choices: Paul’s preaching threatened the silver shrine trade for Artemis
questions.explanation: His business of silver shrines was threatened (Acts 19:24–27).

questions.prompt: What happened to Eutychus at Troas?
choices: He fell from a window and Paul restored him to life
questions.explanation: Eutychus fell and was picked up dead; Paul threw himself on him and he lived (Acts 20:9–12).

questions.prompt: Whom did Paul meet at Miletus?
choices: The elders of the church in Ephesus
questions.explanation: He sent for the elders of the church at Ephesus (Acts 20:17).

questions.prompt: What charge did Paul give the Ephesian elders?
choices: Keep watch over themselves and all the flock as shepherds
questions.explanation: Acts 20:28 calls them to shepherd the church of God.

title: Bound for Jesus’ Name in Jerusalem
lesson: Warned by prophets—including Agabus who binds his own hands with Paul’s belt—Paul still goes up to Jerusalem, ready not only to be bound but to die for the name of the Lord Jesus. James and the elders rejoice at God’s work among the Gentiles and urge Paul to join purification rites to quiet rumors among Jewish believers.

Jews from Asia stir a temple mob, claiming Paul defiled the holy place. Roman soldiers rescue him as the crowd shouts. On the steps Paul tells his conversion story in Aramaic: persecutor, Damascus light, Ananias, and his call to the Gentiles. When he mentions that call, the crowd erupts again. Citizenship and courage meet a hostile city.

featuredVerse.text: Then Paul answered, “Why are you weeping and breaking my heart? I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”

questions.prompt: What did Agabus do with Paul’s belt?
choices: Bound his own hands and feet, saying the owner would be bound in Jerusalem
questions.explanation: Agabus prophesied Paul’s binding in Jerusalem (Acts 21:11).

questions.prompt: How did Paul respond to those urging him not to go?
choices: He said he was ready to be bound and even to die for Jesus’ name
questions.explanation: Acts 21:13 shows Paul’s resolve.

questions.prompt: What accusation sparked the temple riot?
choices: That he brought Greeks into the temple and defiled it
questions.explanation: They claimed he brought Greeks into the temple and defiled the holy place (Acts 21:28).

questions.prompt: In what language did Paul address the crowd from the steps?
questions.explanation: He spoke to them in Aramaic, and they became quieter (Acts 21:40–22:2).

questions.prompt: What part of Paul’s testimony made the crowd shout again?
choices: The Lord’s sending him to the Gentiles
questions.explanation: When he mentioned being sent far away to the Gentiles, they raised their voices (Acts 22:21–22).

title: Councils, Plots, and a Clear Conscience
lesson: Before the Sanhedrin, Paul declares he has fulfilled his duty to God in all good conscience. Division between Pharisees and Sadducees erupts over resurrection hope. That night the Lord stands near Paul: “Take courage! As you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome.” A murderous plot is exposed by Paul’s nephew; soldiers escort him safely to Felix in Caesarea.

Tertullus accuses Paul of being a troublemaker; Paul calmly defends his worship and hope in the resurrection. Felix, familiar with the Way, delays judgment, often talks with Paul, and hopes for a bribe. Two years pass. The gospel is not silenced by politics—Paul keeps speaking about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come.

featuredVerse.text: The following night the Lord stood near Paul and said, “Take courage! As you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome.”

questions.prompt: What did the Lord tell Paul at night after the Sanhedrin hearing?
choices: Take courage—you must also testify in Rome
questions.explanation: Acts 23:11 promises testimony in Rome.

questions.prompt: How was the plot to kill Paul discovered?
choices: Paul’s nephew heard of it and reported it
questions.explanation: The son of Paul’s sister heard of the plot (Acts 23:16).

questions.prompt: Where was Paul taken for safety and trial under Felix?
questions.explanation: Soldiers brought him to Caesarea to Governor Felix (Acts 23:23–35).

questions.prompt: What hope did Paul emphasize in his defense?
choices: Hope in the resurrection of the dead
questions.explanation: Paul spoke of the resurrection of the dead as his hope (Acts 23:6; 24:15).

questions.prompt: Why did Felix keep Paul in custody so long?
choices: He was convinced Paul was innocent and released him immediately
He delayed, often listened, and hoped for a bribe; Paul remained two years
questions.explanation: Felix left Paul in prison for two years, hoping for money (Acts 24:25–27).

title: Appeal to Caesar; Witness Before a King
lesson: Festus succeeds Felix. Jewish leaders renew charges; Paul insists he has done nothing wrong against Jewish law, the temple, or Caesar. To avoid a biased Jerusalem trial, Paul appeals to Caesar. King Agrippa and Bernice arrive, and Festus admits he has nothing definite to write to the emperor about this prisoner.

Before Agrippa, Paul recounts his devout past, the Damascus vision, and his obedience to the heavenly vision—preaching repentance to Jews and Gentiles. He asks why it should be thought incredible that God raises the dead. Agrippa is almost persuaded; Festus calls Paul insane. Yet they agree he could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar. Chains cannot cancel the mission.

featuredVerse.text: So then, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the vision from heaven.

questions.prompt: Why did Paul appeal to Caesar?
choices: He wanted a vacation in Rome
To avoid being handed over for a biased trial in Jerusalem
questions.explanation: Paul refused to go to Jerusalem and appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:9–12).

questions.prompt: Before whom did Paul give his extended testimony in Acts 26?
questions.explanation: Paul spoke before King Agrippa (Acts 26:1–2).

questions.prompt: What did Paul say he was not disobedient to?
questions.explanation: Acts 26:19: he was not disobedient to the heavenly vision.

questions.prompt: What did Agrippa say after Paul’s appeal?
choices: Do you think that in such a short time you can persuade me to be a Christian?
Paul is free to leave Judea forever
questions.explanation: Agrippa’s famous reply is in Acts 26:28.

questions.prompt: What did Agrippa and Festus conclude about Paul?
choices: He had done nothing deserving death or imprisonment; he could have been free if he had not appealed to Caesar
questions.explanation: They agreed he had done nothing deserving death or chains (Acts 26:31–32).

title: Storm, Shipwreck, and an Unhindered Gospel
lesson: Sailing for Rome, Paul warns of disaster, but the centurion listens to the pilot. A violent storm named Euroclydon drives the ship. An angel tells Paul that he must stand before Caesar and that God has graciously given him the lives of all aboard. Paul urges them to eat; the ship runs aground; all 276 reach shore safely on Malta.

On the island, a viper bites Paul without harm; he heals Publius’s father and many others. In Rome, Paul is allowed to live under guard, explains the hope of Israel to Jewish leaders, and for two years welcomes all who come—proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance. The book ends with an open door, not a closed cell.

featuredVerse.text: He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance!

questions.prompt: What assurance did an angel give Paul in the storm?
choices: He must stand before Caesar, and God had given him all those sailing with him
They should jump overboard at once
questions.explanation: Acts 27:23–24 records the angel’s message.

questions.prompt: How many people were aboard and reached land safely?
questions.explanation: There were 276 aboard, and all were brought safely to land (Acts 27:37, 44).

questions.prompt: On which island were they shipwrecked?
questions.explanation: They learned the island was called Malta (Acts 28:1).

questions.prompt: What happened when a viper fastened on Paul’s hand?
choices: He threw the island into panic forever
questions.explanation: He suffered no ill effects, and people changed their minds about him (Acts 28:3–6).

questions.prompt: How does Acts describe Paul’s ministry in Rome at the end?
choices: Proclaiming the kingdom and teaching about Jesus with all boldness and without hindrance
questions.explanation: Acts 28:31 closes with bold, unhindered proclamation.
